title: What ADHD Meds Do (and What They Can't)

shots.voiceover: ADHD medication doesn't give you focus. It gives you the ability to choose where your focus goes.
shots.textOverlay: meds != focus. meds = choosing where focus goes.

shots.voiceover: First week on meds, a lot of people with ADHD describe the same thing: an eerie quiet. No racing thoughts. They do the dishes, open their email, start a task they've avoided for months. Then week two: the med wears off at 4pm and everything they didn't finish is still there.
shots.textOverlay: the quiet is real. but it's not magic.
shots.brollSearch: person focused working desk calm quiet

shots.voiceover: Stimulant medications — Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse — work by increasing dopamine and norepinephrine availability in the prefrontal cortex. This raises baseline executive function: planning, initiating, sustaining attention, and filtering distraction. What they don't do: create motivation that isn't there, fix the executive function habits that ADHD made harder to build, or work past their pharmacological window. Medication is a floor, not a ceiling.
shots.textOverlay: raises the floor -- doesn't replace the skills

shots.voiceover: This is why systems matter even when you're medicated. The medication gives you the window. What you do inside that window — what structure you build — determines whether you hit your ceiling or just your floor. ADHD tools work best when they meet you inside that window. BoxDay is a system for the window.
shots.textOverlay: medication opens the window. systems decide what happens inside it.
